news.headline: A Teen's Beetle Photo Wins a Big Prize
news.body: Oscar Whitfield, a young photographer from the UK who lives in Zimbabwe, won the Natural History Museum's Young Wildlife Photographer of the Year award for 2026. His black-and-white picture, called "Labour of Love," shows a dung beetle pushing a ball of animal poo across the sand in Zambezi National Park. Oscar lay flat on the ground so his camera was at the beetle's eye level. Amelie Davis, also from the UK, won the 10-and-under prize with a colorful bee photo she snapped on her dad's phone.

news.headline: Timekeepers May Swap Leap Seconds for a Leap Hour
news.body: Since 1972, experts have added an extra "leap second" to our clocks 27 times so atomic time stays lined up with Earth's slightly wobbly spin. Computers sometimes get confused by those sudden extra seconds. This week, international timekeepers are voting on whether to stop leap seconds and someday use a "leap hour" instead. That big one-hour fix might not be needed for more than a thousand years.

news.headline: Student-Built Satellites Ride a Rocket to Space
news.body: Two tiny CubeSats built by university students launched toward the International Space Station aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket carrying NASA cargo. The satellites are part of a multi-school project that teaches young engineers how spacecraft work, using shared open designs. Once they leave the station, the CubeSats will test radio messages and even try sending signals between satellites. NASA's CubeSat Launch Initiative helps student teams get their inventions into orbit.

fun_fact: Some dung beetles roll their balls in a straight line by checking the glow of the Milky Way. They're among the only animals known to navigate using our galaxy's band of light! 🌌
